correctness.rationale: In characteristic three linear changes preserve the cubic-power ideal, and every symmetric quadratic form is diagonalizable by congruence. A nonzero square-variable factor is J_2[0] plus J_1[1]. Three direct primitive tensor identities were proved from explicit homogeneous generators, yielding the three recurrences and closed polynomials for all r; inactive factors multiply by T. The quotient length strictly decreases for positive rank and symmetric form counts follow from radical choice and standard finite orthogonal group order formulas. Actual standalone verify.py recomputes multiplication maps and chain generator degrees for all 729 ternary three-variable forms and additional GF9/GF3 tests, returning VERIFY_OK. These computations corroborate, not replace, the induction and orbit counts.

originality.rationale: The graded degree-start classification is not implied by the explicitly compared ungraded primitive tensor decomposition alone: forgetting gradings loses all starting-degree data. Nor is multiplication by an arbitrary quadratic form generally a power of a linear form when the polar rank exceeds one. The result combines a new explicit graded all-rank decomposition with exact distinct quotient Hilbert series and finite-field frequencies. Searches did not find the full theorem, though absence of a search hit is not proof of novelty; possible specialized graded tensor/Hilbert-function coverage is a residual risk.

value.rationale: Graded multiplication by quadratic forms in truncated group algebras is a natural deformation and Hilbert-series problem: ungraded Jordan block lengths do not encode quotient degrees. The result classifies all possible graded strings and Hilbert functions for every dimension n>=3 and finite extension field of characteristic three, resolves their exact rank distribution and finite-field point counts, and identifies a strict chain of n+1 distinct graded strata. It is a complete natural classification, not a trivial isolated parameter computation; no downstream theorem is claimed.
